## Skill loaded

**`craft:review-loop`**. The global prompt sends every review step to this skill, and it replaces `superpowers:receiving-code-review`. Ponytail is already on from the session hook. No other skill applies yet. `craft:github` comes in only at the fix commit, and the repo has no GitHub remote, so there is nothing to file.

## What the agent does next with the finding

1. **Count it.** The finding fails only in one state: the icon service has only its placeholder. So the global rule asks for a count against the real data. `data/brands.csv` has the result of a check from 2026-09:
   - 76 of 1000 brands get only the placeholder.
   - 7 of those 76 have a usable icon on their own site (`brand994` to `brand1000`).

   The count is 7, not zero, so the finding stands. The agent sends a Haiku subagent to count; I had no Agent tool here, so I counted with `awk`.
2. **Classify it.** It is a defect: real use reaches a wrong result. For those 7 rows the branch makes things worse. Before, the row showed the placeholder. Now the CSP blocks the redirect and the row shows a broken image. So round 1 confirms a defect. Its fix becomes one commit, and round 2 reads only that commit.
3. **Ask, do not fix.** There is no single obvious fix. Each fix changes what users see, loosens the CSP (a permission rule) or changes the data the product keeps. That is business logic (step 4 of *The findings*). The agent gives options and a recommendation.
4. **End the turn on the question.** Nothing else in round 1 can go on. There is no other finding. There is no architecture file and no ADR folder, so no architecture review runs beside round 1. Round 2 cannot start, because it reads the fix commit, and the fix depends on the answer.
5. **After the answer:**
   - Write the test first and see it fail on `adff96c`.
   - Write the fix and run `npm test`.
   - Commit through `craft:github`.
   - Run round 2 on that commit: `/code-review high <sha>^..<sha>`. If the person picks option D, which is a fix to security code, run it at `xhigh`.

   The agent sends no message between the answer and round 2.

When I checked the finding, I also found two defects that the review did not report. They change what each option costs, so they go into the question.

## The one message before round 2

> **Round 1 of the review (`/code-review high`, whole branch) found one defect. The fix needs your decision.**
>
> **The defect.** `public/index.html` lets images load only from `'self'` and `https://icons.example.com`. The new fallback in `src/server.js` redirects `/logo` to an icon on the brand's own site. The browser blocks that image, so the fallback never shows an icon.
>
> **Who it affects.** `data/brands.csv` has the result of a check from 2026-09:
> - 76 of 1000 brands get only the placeholder.
> - 7 of those 76 have a usable icon on their own site: `brand994` to `brand1000`.
>
> For those 7, the branch makes the row worse. Before, the row showed the placeholder. Now it shows a broken image.
>
> **Two more defects in the same new code.** The review did not report them. I found them when I checked the finding.
> - **Crash:** if a `fetch` in `/logo` fails, for example because a brand site is down, Node 24 stops the server. I reproduced this with a small handler of the same form whose `fetch` fails.
> - **Open redirect:** `/logo` takes `domain` from the query string and does not check it against `brands.csv`. The server then fetches `https://<domain>/` and redirects to the icon link on that page. So anyone can use the site as an open redirect, and can make the server request any HTTPS host.
>
> Also, every `/logo` request now sends a `HEAD` request to the icon service first. That is 1000 requests for each view of the page.
>
> **Options.**
> - **A. Remove the fallback (revert `adff96c`).**
>   - The 7 brands show the placeholder, as before the branch.
>   - The crash, the open redirect and the `HEAD` requests go away.
>   - The branch then has no change.
> - **B. Keep the 7 icons in the repository.**
>   - At start, the server loads a fixed list from `brands.csv`. `/logo` returns the stored icon from the site's own origin, which the CSP allows.
>   - The query string never builds a path or a URL, and nothing is fetched at run time. So the crash, the open redirect and the `HEAD` requests go away.
>   - Limit: a new placeholder brand, or a brand that changes its icon, needs a manual update, as the `own` column does today.
> - **C. Change `img-src` to allow `https:`.**
>   - A one-line change.
>   - The page then loads images from any HTTPS host, and each view sends users' browsers to the brand sites.
>   - The crash and the open redirect stay and need their own fixes.
> - **D. Fetch the brand's icon through the server and return it from the site's origin.**
>   - More code.
>   - The server then serves content from any host as its own, so it needs SSRF protection and a check of the content type.
>   - The review of that fix runs at `xhigh`.
>
> **My recommendation: B.** It shows the icon for every brand that the data says has one. It keeps the CSP as it is. It removes the crash and the open redirect with the least code. If 7 icons are not worth maintaining a set of files, choose A.
>
> After you answer, I write the test first. On `adff96c` it fails: `/logo` for `brand994.example` gives an image that the page's CSP blocks. Then I make the fix, run `npm test` and commit. Round 2 of the review reads only that commit.

I changed no files and ran no review. I only read files and ran one throwaway Node process that wrote nothing to the repo. `git status` is still clean.
